title: Tharu Culture in Chitwan: Villages, Dance and Food
meta_description: Tharu culture in Chitwan: who the Tharu are, village houses and art, stick dance, Maghi festival, Tharu food such as dhikri and ghonghi, and how to visit respectfully.
summary: The Tharu are among the oldest peoples of Nepal's Terai and the original farmers of Chitwan. Visitors can meet their culture through village walks, the Tharu Cultural Museum and stick dance in Sauraha, a homestay in Barauli, and festivals such as Maghi in January. Go with a local guide and ask before taking photos.

sections.heading: Who the Tharu are
paras: The Tharu are an indigenous people spread along the Terai from the far west of Nepal to the east, and across the border into India. They are one of Nepal's largest ethnic groups, with several distinct communities, dialects and customs; the Tharu of Chitwan differ from the Rana and Dangaura Tharu of the far west in language, dress and dance. For centuries they farmed clearings in the malaria-ridden forests, and they had a reputation for resistance to the disease that kept most hill people away.

That changed in the 1950s and 1960s, when malaria eradication opened Chitwan to settlers from the hills and land was cleared for farming. The creation of the national park in 1973 removed further land and forest rights. Many Tharu families lost land in these decades, and in the far west, the kamaiya bonded-labour system that tied many Tharu families to landlords was only abolished in 2000. Today Tharu communities are active in community forestry, buffer-zone management and tourism around the park.

sections.heading: Village life and houses
paras: A traditional Chitwan Tharu house is low and long, with walls of woven reed or wood plastered with mud and cow dung, and a roof of thatch or tiles. Inside, rooms are divided by large clay grain containers, sometimes taller than a person, called dehari, that store rice for the year. Walls and doorways are often decorated with clay reliefs and paintings of birds, elephants, deer and plants, renewed at festivals.

Life follows the farming calendar. Rice is planted with the monsoon in June and July and harvested in October and November; mustard and wheat follow in winter, and fields turn yellow in January. Fishing in rivers and ponds with handmade bamboo traps and nets is an important part of daily life, particularly for women. Many families also keep buffalo, goats and pigs, and villages have shared shrines to local deities at the edge of the settlement.

sections.heading: A half-day village visit, step by step
paras: The most popular way to see Tharu village life from Sauraha is a guided bicycle ride or walk of 2.5–3 hours, costing about NPR 1,500 per person with guide and bike. Routes run west and north of Sauraha through Bachhauli and neighbouring hamlets, on flat dirt lanes between rice and mustard fields, with a total distance of 8–12 km by bike.

A good guide stops at a working household to show the grain stores and clay reliefs, explains how the bamboo fish traps and nets are made and used, and introduces you to the family rather than walking you through like a tourist sight. Many rides also pass a community forest office, a school and a village shrine, and end at the Tharu Cultural Museum or a riverside tea stall. Go at 7–8 am or after 3 pm from March onwards to avoid the heat, and in December and January wait until the fog lifts, usually by 10 am.
list: Wear closed shoes and carry water; lanes can be dusty or muddy
Ask your guide to arrange a cup of tea in a home, and pay the family directly
Allow extra time in January for Maghi visits, when families welcome guests with food

sections.heading: Dance and music
paras: The best-known Tharu dance is the lathi naach or stick dance, performed by lines of men, sometimes with women, who strike bamboo sticks against their partners' in an increasingly fast rhythm to the madal drum and song. Explanations of its origin vary; a common one is that villagers used sticks to drive away wild animals and evil spirits from fields and homes. Other dances include the peacock dance, with a costumed dancer imitating the bird, and harvest dances performed by women in white with red borders.

In Sauraha, the Tharu Culture House and several hotels stage these dances most evenings, usually around 7 pm, with tickets of a few hundred rupees. They are staged for visitors, but performers are local young people who also dance at village festivals. For a less formal setting, the courtyard dances at the Barauli homestay or a visit during Maghi show the dances as part of community life.

sections.heading: Tharu food to try
paras: Tharu cooking is simple, seasonal and built on rice, fish and fresh greens, with mustard oil, garlic, turmeric and chilli. Some dishes appear on restaurant menus in Sauraha; others you will only taste in a home or homestay.
list: Dhikri: steamed rice-flour dough shaped into rolls or figures, eaten with chutney or curry, especially at festivals
Ghonghi: freshwater snails cooked in a spicy, herby sauce, sucked from the shell
Fish curry or fried fish from rivers and ponds, often caught in bamboo traps
Bagiya: a dumpling similar to dhikri, often filled, made in some Tharu communities
Seasonal greens and pickles, and in some homes, homemade rice beer at festivals

sections.heading: Crafts, dress and what to buy
paras: Tharu households make much of what they use. Women weave colourful baskets, lidded boxes and fans from grass and reeds, often dyed in bright pinks, greens and yellows, and men make bamboo fish traps, sieves and stools. Older women in some villages still have tattoos on their arms and legs, applied when they were young as a mark of identity and beauty, a practice now rare among younger generations.

Festival dress for women typically pairs a wrap skirt or lehenga with a short blouse, heavy silver necklaces, anklets and bangles, while men wear a dhoti and vest for dances. In Sauraha and Barauli you can buy baskets, small reed boxes, woven bags and clay figures from community shops and the women's groups that run the homestay. Prices are low, typically a few hundred to a couple of thousand rupees, so bargaining hard is out of place.

sections.heading: Festivals in the Tharu year
paras: The most important Tharu festival is Maghi, celebrated on the first day of the Nepali month of Magh, usually 14 or 15 January, at the same time as Makar Sankranti. It marks the Tharu new year: families bathe early, prepare feasts with dhikri, fish and meat, visit elders for blessings and dance through the night. In the past, Maghi was also when work contracts and village responsibilities were renewed.

Other festivals include Fagu, the Tharu version of Holi in spring, and Diwali in autumn, plus Hindu festivals such as Dashain and Tihar that are widely celebrated. Visiting Chitwan around Maghi, combined with Makar Sankranti at Devghat, gives a rich picture of the region's festival life.

sections.heading: Visiting respectfully
paras: Tharu villages are homes, not museums. A local guide, ideally from the community, makes visits more welcome and more meaningful, and makes sure the benefit stays local.
list: Ask before photographing people, entering courtyards or looking inside houses
Dress modestly in villages; cover shoulders and knees
Do not give money or sweets to children; support schools or community funds instead
Buy crafts and food directly from villagers or community projects
Choose homestays run by the community, such as Barauli, rather than staged villages

faqs.q: Who are the Tharu people of Chitwan?
faqs.a: The Tharu are an indigenous people of Nepal's Terai and among the oldest communities in Chitwan. They farmed the forest edges for centuries and were known for resistance to malaria. They have their own languages, customs, dances, house styles and festivals, and today play a central role in community forestry and tourism around the park.

faqs.q: Where can I see the Tharu stick dance in Chitwan?
faqs.a: At the Tharu Culture House in Sauraha, most evenings around 7 pm, and at several hotels. Tickets cost about NPR 200–300. For a more informal performance, the Barauli homestay's village group dances in the courtyard for guests, and villages dance at Maghi in mid-January.

faqs.q: What is the Tharu Cultural Museum in Sauraha?
faqs.a: A small museum on the edge of Sauraha that explains Tharu farming, fishing, festivals, clothing and house-building through photographs, tools and life-size wall art. It takes about an hour and is a useful introduction before a village walk or homestay.

faqs.q: Can I stay in a Tharu village near Chitwan?
faqs.a: Yes. The Barauli Community Homestay in Nawalpur, run by Tharu women since 2015, offers private cottages with attached bathrooms and meals with host families. Our Tharu culture homestay package includes two nights there plus a night in Sauraha with a canoe safari.

Maghi is the Tharu new year, celebrated on the first day of the Nepali month of Magh, usually 14 or 15 January. Families bathe, feast on dhikri, fish and meat, visit elders for blessings and dance. It coincides with Makar Sankranti, when Hindus bathe at Devghat.

faqs.q: What Tharu food should I try?
faqs.a: Try dhikri, steamed rice-flour dumplings, ghonghi, freshwater snails in spicy sauce, and fish curry. Some Sauraha restaurants serve Tharu dishes, but the best place to taste them is a homestay, where you can help cook. Vegetarian Tharu meals are also available.

faqs.q: Is a Tharu village tour ethical?
faqs.a: It can be, if done respectfully with a local guide, short visits, permission for photos and money going to the community. Community-run homestays such as Barauli are a good model. Avoid tours that treat villages as attractions or pay nothing to residents.

faqs.q: How did the national park affect the Tharu?
faqs.a: The creation of Chitwan National Park in 1973, after decades of settlement from the hills, reduced Tharu access to forest, grazing and fishing, and some villages were moved. Today buffer-zone programmes share part of park income with local communities, and many Tharu work in tourism and conservation.

faqs.q: What should I wear when visiting a Tharu village?
faqs.a: Light, modest clothing that covers shoulders and knees, comfortable shoes you can get muddy, and a hat in hot months. Remove shoes if invited into a home. In winter evenings bring a warm layer, as temperatures drop quickly after sunset.
